issues.legal_issue: A High Court exercising second-appellate jurisdiction cannot reappraise evidence and replace a lower appellate court’s finding of fact with its own finding.
material_facts: After remand, the first appellate court found on the evidence and circumstances that the suit was barred by limitation.
In a later second appeal, the High Court reassessed the evidence and reversed that finding.
The Supreme Court held that the limitation finding was one of fact and that the High Court had exceeded its second-appellate role.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not replace the first appellate court’s factual finding on limitation; its judgment was set aside and the decree dismissing the suit as time-barred was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a High Court in second appeal cannot make a fresh appraisal of evidence to reach a different conclusion on a factual finding. The Court cited no earlier cases for this principle.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal to a High Court from a lower appellate court’s decision.
predicates.first_appellate_finding_based_on_evidenc: The lower appellate court made a factual finding after considering the evidence and circumstances.
predicates.high_court_reappraised_evidence: The High Court reassessed the evidence to reach a different factual conclusion.

issues.definition: When a second appeal concerns a factual finding made after assessment of evidence, and the High Court reassesses that evidence, the High Court must not replace the finding with its own.

issues.legal_issue: An alleged admission cannot be relied on selectively by using only part of it and disregarding the rest.
material_facts: The High Court relied on what it treated as the defendant’s admission in the written statement when reversing the first appellate court’s finding on limitation.
The Supreme Court stated that, if the High Court relied on the alleged admission, it had to consider the admission as a whole rather than rely on only part of it.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not rely on a part of the alleged admission while ignoring the remainder.
issues.legal_principle: An admission relied on by a court must be taken as a whole; a court may not selectively rely on one part and disregard another. The Court cited no provision or earlier case for this principle.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal to a High Court from a lower appellate court’s decision.
predicates.high_court_relied_on_partial_admission: The High Court used only part of an alleged admission while disregarding other parts of it.

issues.definition: When a High Court in a second appeal relies on only part of an alleged admission, it must consider the admission as a whole.

issues.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking relief on the basis of title must establish the plaintiff’s own title and cannot succeed merely because the defendant has not proved title.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a declaration of title and possession based on an alleged settlement of the disputed land.
The Supreme Court stated that the plaintiff had to prove title on the basis of that settlement and that the defendant was not obliged to prove title in the case.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff bore the burden of proving the title on which the claim was based; the plaintiff had to succeed on the strength of that case.
issues.legal_principle: A party seeking relief on title must establish its own title rather than rely on a failure by the opposing party to establish title. The Court cited no provision or earlier case for this principle.

predicates.title_and_possession_suit: The proceeding is a suit in which the plaintiff seeks relief concerning title and possession of property.
predicates.plaintiff_claimed_title_from_own_source: The plaintiff bases the claimed title on a source of title asserted by the plaintiff.

issues.definition: In a suit concerning title and possession, when the plaintiff claims title from an asserted source, the plaintiff must establish that own title.
